## Paper

## Abstract

Inducing antigen-specific regulatory T (Treg) cells is a promising strategy for treating autoimmune diseases (AID). Here, we present dendritic cells-CD4⁺ T cells (DC-CD4) bispecific tolerogenic nanovesicles (NV) co-loaded with an antigenic peptide and rapamycin. We show that these NVs bring DCs and CD4⁺ T cells into close spatial proximity through CTLA4-CD80/86 and anti-CD4 (aCD4)-CD4 interactions, thereby promoting antigen-specific Treg cell generation. In a collagen-induced arthritis mouse model, the bispecific NVs display enhanced lymph node (LN) tropism and increase antigen-specific Treg cells in LNs and spleen, when administered in both therapeutic and prophylactic settings, resulting in robust efficacy against CIA. Furthermore, arthritogenic cell transfer and adoptive transfer of Treg cells into Treg-ablated mice confirm the pivotal role of bispecific NV-induced antigen-specific Treg cells in mediating the anti-inflammatory efficacy. Collectively, our data support DC-CD4 bispecific tolerogenic NVs as a platform to induce antigen-specific Treg cells for precise immune tolerance in AIDs.

---

## Introduction

Immune tolerance refers to the immune system’s ability to distinguish self from non-self, actively preventing immune responses against the body’s own tissues1-3. This mechanism is essential for maintaining immune homeostasis and preventing immune disorders1, 3. In recent years, the concept of therapeutically inducing immune tolerance has garnered increasing attention as a promising strategy for treating autoimmune disorders4-7, allergies8, 9, and transplant rejection10, 11. Being distinct from conventional immunosuppression that broadly dampens immunity, restoring immune tolerance offers significant advantages in terms of antigen-specificity (targeting only pathogenic immune responses), long-term efficacy (reprogramming immune memory), and minimal systemic toxicity (preserving host defense against infections)1, 12. Therefore, immune tolerance is an attractive therapeutic strategy for a wide range of immune-mediated conditions.

Regulatory T (Treg) cells, a specialized subset of CD4+ T lymphocytes characterized by Foxp3 expression, play a pivotal role in maintaining immune tolerance and preventing autoimmune disorders13-17. Current clinical strategies in Treg-mediated immunotherapy primarily focus on two major approaches: direct adoptive transfer of ex vivo-expanded Treg cells 18, 19 and in vivo induction of endogenous Treg cells using tolerogenic dendritic cells (tDC)20, 21 or Treg-biased immunostimulants such as IL-2 variants17. However, cell-based approaches face significant challenges, including the patient-specific production in a clinical setup and labor-intensive process of in vitro cell expansion, induction and reinfusion22-24. To overcome these limitations, nanotechnology-based strategies have been explored to deliver antigens and immunosuppressive agents specifically to antigen presenting cells (APC), particularly dendritic cells (DC), thereby boosting the generation of antigen-specific Treg cells in situ4, 6, 12, 25, 26. Among these approaches, Sohn et al. reported lipid nanoparticles (LNP) co-loaded with type II collagen peptide and rapamycin (RM), which reduced synovial inflammation and ameliorated osteoarthritis in mice, providing a compelling proof-of-concept for NP-mediated antigen-specific tolerance in joint disease6. However, this strategy relies on passive uptake by DCs followed by intradermal (i.d.) injection, without actively targeting or programming DC fate to coordinate crosstalk with other immune cells. Therefore, there is an urgent need to develop a targeted tolerogenic strategy that actively reprograms DCs and amplifies their interactions with immune partners, driving more efficient and durable induction of antigen-specific Treg cells.

Bispecific systems, such as bispecific NPs and antibodies, have emerged as innovative tools capable of bridging distinct immune cell types to enhance intercellular communication27-31. By simultaneously engaging specific receptors on both types of cells, these systems can precisely orchestrate cellular crosstalk27, 28. To date, bispecific strategies have been extensively explored in cancer therapies, where they are primarily used to link immune effector cells with tumor cells, thereby promoting immune-mediated tumor eradication27-31. Nevertheless, their application in non-cancer settings to induce immune tolerance, particularly in inflammatory diseases such as autoimmune diseases (AID), remains limited. Considering the critical role of cellular crosstalk in shaping inflammatory responses, there is significant potential for harnessing bispecific nanosystem to modulate pathological immune interactions in these contexts. Therefore, developing bispecific nanoplatforms tailored for inflammatory disease intervention via generating antigen-specific Treg cells represents a promising yet underexplored frontier.

Here we develop a DC-CD4 bispecific tolerogenic nanovesicle (NV) platform that actively couples DCs with CD4⁺ T cells to enhance tolerogenic crosstalk and drive antigen-specific Treg cell induction in vivo. The platform enhances lymph node (LN) accumulation after i.d. administration, strengthens DC-CD4 engagement, and amplifies antigen-specific Treg responses in lymphoid organs. These effects support a coordinated tolerogenic program that promotes tDC differentiation, immunosuppressive CD4+ T cell (iCD4) induction, and subsequent antigen-specific Treg cell generation. Collectively, these activities establish durable, antigen-specific immune tolerance in a collagen-induced arthritis model. This work provides a generalizable strategy for programming immune cell interactions to achieve precise immune tolerance, and offers a modular framework for antigen-specific immunotherapy across autoimmune and other immune-mediated inflammatory diseases.

---

## Results

1 Preparation and characterization of CII-RM@aCD4Tn
The fabrication process for CII-RM@aCD4Tn encapsulating bovine type II collagen 259 to 273 peptide (CII) is shown in Fig. 1a. iCD4 with stabled high CTLA4 express were successfully induced from CD4+ T cells isolated from spleen and LNs, showing approximately threefold expansion at 10 ng mL-1 TGF-β (Supplementary Fig. 1a-e). Additionally, the key immunomodulatory markers PD-1 (P<0.0001) and LAG-3 (P=0.0012) were significantly upregulated following stimulation (Supplementary Fig. 1f). For CII-RM@aCD4Tn preparation, NVs derived from iCD4 (referred to as Tn) were prepared through sequential extrusion and used for LN-targeted delivery (Supplementary Fig. 2). Protein analysis confirmed that Tn shared a protein expression profile closely mirroring that of parent iCD4 (Supplementary Fig. 3).

To optimize the binding affinity of CII-RM@aCD4Tn to CD4+ T cells, DP-aCD4 were synthesized with varying reaction molar ratios of DSPE-PEG2000-NHS (DP) to anti-CD4 Fab fragment (aCD4). Membrane insertion capacity of DP-aCD4 on CD4+ T cells reached a plateau of approximately 100% when the molar ratio up to 8 (Supplementary Fig. 4a). Nevertheless, when the reaction molar ratio exceeded 8, the affinity of CII-RM@aCD4Tn for CD4+ T cells gradually declined with increased DP modification on aCD4 (Supplementary Fig. 4b), primarily due to partial functional inactivation of aCD4. Consequently, a DP:aCD4 ratio of 8:1 was selected as optimal, yielding CII-RM@aCD4Tn with efficient attachment to CD4+ T cell membrane (Supplementary Fig. 4c).

Under these conditions, CII-RM@aCD4Tn loaded with CII and rapamycin (RM), and functionalized with aCD4 was successfully fabricated (Fig. 1b), with spherical morphology and integrated structure around 130 nm under TEM detection (Fig. 1c). CII-RM@aCD4Tn had a hydrodynamic diameter of 165.7 nm with a Zeta potential of -16.1 mV (Fig. 1d,e). Release of CII and RM from CII-RM@aCD4Tn was quantified by ELISA and HPLC (Supplementary Fig. 5a). Encapsulation efficiency and drug loading capacity of CII and RM were demonstrated in Supplementary Fig. 5b, with CII-RM@aCD4Tn displaying sustained drug release over 24 h (Supplementary Fig. 5c). Long-term stability assessments exhibited that CII-RM@aCD4Tn retained structural integrity when stored in PBS or serum for up to 7 days (Supplementary Fig. 6a,b). Moreover, cryopreservation studies further confirmed their resilience, with no significant changes in particle size or biofunctional activity after 3 weeks of storage at -80℃. (Supplementary Fig. 6c,d).

2 CII-RM@aCD4Tn-mediated immunosuppression in DCs and CD4+ T cells
To determine the efficiency of Tn in enhancing the delivery of drugs (CII and RM) to DCs, FITC-labelled free drugs or CII-RM@aCD4Tn were incubated with bone marrow-derived dendritic cells (BMDC) on an orbital shaker at 40 rpm for 12 h. While all cells internalized CII and RM, drug uptake was 2.7-fold higher when the agents were encapsulated in Tn compared to the free form (Fig. 1f,g). The enhanced uptake by BMDCs are mainly attributable to more efficient ligand-mediated interactions between CII-RM@aCD4Tn and BMDCs. To assess antigen (CII) presentation on DC surface, FITC-labelled CII were incubated with BMDCs on an orbital shaker for 24 h. CII-RM@aCD4Tn facilitated antigen presentation, increasing surface displayed CII levels by 3.1-fold compared to free CII (Fig. 1h,i). To examine whether Tn-mediated antigen delivery facilitated processing and presentation via MHC II on the surface of DCs, Eα peptides, which can be detected by Yae antibody upon forming MHC II complex6, were employed in place of CII to generate Eα-RM@aCD4Tn. After co-culture of Eα-RM@aCD4Tn with BMDCs for 24 h, a substantial fraction of Eα peptide was presented on the cell surface via MHC II, resulting in a 5.8-fold increase compared to free Eα (Supplementary Fig. 7).

tDCs are crucial for maintaining immune homeostasis and preventing autoimmune responses20, 21, 25. BMDCs were incubated with various formulations for 48 h, followed by LPS stimulation for 24 h, and the expression of activation markers and cytokines was subsequently analyzed by flow cytometry (FC), ELISA and qRT-PCR. Matured BMDCs (mDC) displayed high expression levels of CD80, CD86, CD40 and MHC II, all of which were significantly reduced following CII-RM@aCD4Tn treatment (all P<0.0001) (Fig. 1j and Supplementary Fig. 8a). Interestingly, PD-L1 expression was markedly upregulated in BMDCs after CII-RM@aCD4Tn treatment compared to mDCs (P<0.0001) (Supplementary Fig. 8a). Furthermore, pro-inflammatory cytokine TNF and its corresponding mRNA level were highest in mDCs, whereas anti-inflammatory cytokine TGF-β and its mRNA expression were lowest, when compared to other groups (Fig. 1k and Supplementary Fig. 8b). Compared to mDCs, CII-RM@aCD4Tn treatment markedly suppressed TNF expression at both the protein and mRNA levels while significantly upregulating TGF-β (all P<0.0001) (Fig. 1k and Supplementary Fig. 8b).

iCD4 including Foxp3⁺ Treg cells and Foxp3⁻ suppressive CD4⁺ subsets, are essential for immune regulation and autoimmunity prevention, holding therapeutic promise for a range of conditions12, 18, 32, 33. To determine whether CII-RM@aCD4Tn could induce iCD4, CD4+ T cells were cultured with it for 48 h and subsequently activated with PMA for 6 h. FC analysis revealed increased expression of CTLA4 and PD-1 with reduced CD127 expression compared to active CD4+ T cells (aCD4) (all P<0.0001) (Fig. 2l and Supplementary Fig. 9a). Moreover, cells treated with CII-RM@aCD4Tn exhibited elevated TGF-β protein and mRNA levels, while TNF expression was significant reduced relative to aCD4 (all P<0.0001) (Fig. 2m and Supplementary Fig. 9b), suggesting successful induction of a immunosuppressive phenotype.

Together, these findings indicate that CII-RM@aCD4Tn promotes the differentiation of tDCs and iCD4, enhancing anti-inflammatory cytokine secretion while suppressing pro-inflammatory responses.

3 Bridging effects of CII-RM@aCD4Tn on CD4+ T cells and DCs
CD4 molecules on CD4+ T cells and CD80/86 co-stimulatory molecules on DCs represent stable surface biomarkers, making them suitable targets for CII-RM@aCD4Tn engagement (Fig. 2a). Equal numbers of CD4+ T cells and BMDCs were co-incubated for 1 h with either CII-RM@Tn or CII-RM@aCD4Tn. FC analysis of DC-CD4 conjugates showed that, in the presence of CII-RM@Tn, CD4⁺ T cells and BMDCs largely remained as single, unpaired cells, whereas CII-RM@aCD4Tn markedly increased the proportion of BMDC-CD4⁺ T cell pairs compared to CII-RM@Tn group (P<0.0001) (Fig. 2b). To directly evidence CTLA4-CD80/86 interactions between CII-RM@aCD4Tn and BMDCs, we selectively blocked CD80/86 on BMDCs with CTLA4 Ig (G2), CTLA4 on the NV surface with an anti-CTLA4 antibody (G3), or both binding partners simultaneously (G4) (Supplementary Fig. 10a). The frequency of DC-CD4 cell pairs decreased from 38.1% in the unblocked condition to ~8% when either CD80/86 or CTLA4 was blocked individually, and to ~6% when both were blocked (Supplementary Fig. 10b), demonstrating the effective interaction of CII-RM@aCD4Tn and BMDC mediated through CTLA4-CD80/86 axis.

To detect the in vivo gripping ability of CII-RM@aCD4Tn, inguinal LNs (iLN) from DBA/1 mice were collected for immunofluorescence staining after 24 h i.d injection at the flank. Cy5-CII-RM@aCD4Tn localized to CD11c+ DCs and also bound with CD4+ T cells (Fig. 2c). In addition, CII-RM@aCD4Tn promoted interactions between DCs and CD4+ T cells in paracortex of LNs (Fig. 2c). By contrast, CII-RM@Tn primarily resulted in DC-specific internalization without promoting DC-CD4 conjugation (Supplementary Fig. 11). To further identify the in vivo cellular targets, Cy5-CII-RM@aCD4Tn-associated cells were analyzed in iLN. Among Cy5⁺ CD45⁺ leukocytes, NVs were predominantly targeted to CD4+ T cells (44.8%) and CD11c⁺ DCs (31.3%), followed by CD19⁺ B cells (11.7%), whereas uptake by CD11b⁺ macrophages (7.9%) and Ly6G⁺ neutrophils (3.2%) was comparatively low (Supplementary Fig. 12a). When CD4+ T cells were co-cultured with purified APC subsets in the presence of CII-RM@aCD4Tn, CD11c⁺ DCs elicited the highest IL-10 levels in the medium (Supplementary Fig. 12b,c), implying that DCs are the dominant APC subset engaging the NVs to drive tolerogenic responses.

These data support the bispecific capacity of CII-RM@aCD4Tn to simultaneously engage CD4+ T cells and DCs realizing the effective cellular bridging both in vitro and in vivo.

4 Biodistribution and biosafety of CII-RM@aCD4Tn
To assess LN-targeting capability, CII-RM@aCD4Tn were administered via i.d. injection into the left or right flank of DBA/1 mice. Following unilateral injection, in vivo fluorescence imaging revealed that the Cy5-NVs localized exclusively to the ipsilateral iLN and axillary LN (aLN), with minimal signal detected in major organs (Fig. 2d,e and Supplementary Fig. 13). Following bilateral injections, the fluorescence intensity (FI) in iLNs and aLNs account for 80.6% of the total FI, which was significantly higher than unilateral injection (left P=0.0027, right P=0.0001) (Fig. 2f,g). These results indicate that administration at both flanks effectively delivers CII-RM@aCD4Tn to systemic LNs throughout the body, potentially exerting enhance immune modulation. In vivo imaging at different time points after i.d. administration revealed that Cy5-CII-RM@aCD4Tn remained localized near to the injection site for at least one week, whereas free drug (CII + RM) diffused quickly within 4 days (Fig. 2h,i). Quantitative analysis showed that the area under FI curve over one week in CII-RM@aCD4Tn group was 2.8-fold higher than that of free drug group (Supplementary Fig. 14), indicating prolonged local retention of the LNVs. Localization in iLN was further tracked over time. The iLN signal peaked on day 1 and then declined gradually (Fig. 2j,k). On day 7, ~13.1% of the maximal iLN FI remained, falling to near-background levels on day 9 (~3.3%) (Fig. 2k).

For biosafety assessment, male DBA/1 received i.d. injections of the respective formulations (Supplementary Fig. 15a). Blood biochemical analysis demonstrated no significant alterations in the levels of alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and albumin across all groups (Supplementary Fig. 15b), and routine haematological parameters remained within normal physiological ranges (Supplementary Fig. 15c). Furthermore, histological examination of major organs revealed no evidence of tissue damage or inflammation (Supplementary Fig. 15d). These results indicate no detectable systemic or organ toxicity, supporting the overall biocompatibility of the CII-RM@aCD4Tn nanosystem.

5 Antigen-specific immunosuppression mediated by the DC-CD4 bridging system
Given the induction of tDCs and iCD4 by CII-RM@aCD4Tn, we next examined the generation of Treg cells by this system. Considering the high responsiveness of CD4+ T cells from OT-II transgenic mice to chicken ovalbumin 323 to 339 peptides (OVA), we synthesized OVA loaded NVs (OVA-RM@aCD4Tn) and incubated them with OT-II splenocytes in vitro (Supplementary Fig. 16a). FC analysis revealed an increased proportion of CD25+ Foxp3+ Treg cells after OVA-RM@aCD4Tn treatment, with 1.5-fold elevation compared to OVA-RM@Tn group (Supplementary Fig. 16b,c). Moreover, OVA-RM@aCD4Tn treatment suppressed the level of the pro-inflammatory cytokine TNF and enhanced expression of the anti-inflammatory cytokine TGF-β compared to OVA group (both P<0.0001) (Supplementary Fig. 16d).

To clarify the extent of in vivo immunosuppression, different types of NVs were injected i.d. into OT-II mice at both flanks (Fig. 3a). Although the non-antigen containing formulations (G4 and G5) modestly increased the percentage of Treg cells compared to PBS, OVA-RM@aCD4Tn induced the highest proportions and absolute numbers of CD25+ Foxp3+ Treg cells in the LNs, with 9.7-fold and 1.3-fold higher percentages than PBS and OVA-RM@Tn, respectively (Fig. 3b,c and Supplementary Fig. 17). A similar pattern was observed in the spleen, where the OVA-RM@aCD4Tn increased the Treg cell proportion by 8.4-fold and 1.4-fold compared to PBS and OVA-RM@Tn, respectively (Fig. 3b,d and Supplementary Fig. 18). The immunosuppressive efficacy of this system was further evaluated in DBA/1 mice after i.d. injection of CII-loaded NVs (Supplementary Fig. 19a). Consistently, CII-RM@aCD4Tn yielded the highest numbers and proportions of Treg cells in both LNs and spleen among all treatment groups (Supplementary Fig. 19b,c). Taken together, Ag-RM@aCD4Tn platform robustly expands Treg cells in both LNs and spleen.

To determine whether the induced immunosuppression was antigen-specific, splenocytes isolated from OT-II or DBA/1 mice pre-immunized with different formulations were re-stimulated ex vivo with either OVA or CII, and IFN-γ-producing cells in splenocytes were quantified by ELISPOT (Supplementary Fig. 20a). In OT-II mice, OVA restimulation revealed a marked reduction in IFN-γ-secreting cells after pretreatment with OVA-RM@aCD4Tn (G1 vs G2, P<0.0001), corresponding to a 71.6% decrease (Fig. 3e,f). Pretreatment with CII-RM@aCD4Tn produced a 30.5% reduction, which was significantly weaker than that induced by OVA-RM@aCD4Tn (G2 vs G4, P<0.0001) (Fig. 3e,f). However, CII-RM@aCD4Tn also demonstrated a significant reduction in IFN-γ production compared to CII alone in OT-II mice (G3 vs G4, P=0.0001) (Fig. 3e,f), which is likely attributable to the intrinsic baseline immunosuppressive properties of the iCD4-derived NVs. Conversely, in DBA/1 mice, CII restimulation demonstrated that CII-RM@aCD4Tn produced significantly suppression of IFN-γ-producing cells than OVA-RM@aCD4Tn (G2 vs G4, P<0.0001) (Fig. 3g,h). Consistent with these findings, cytokine levels of TNF and TGF-β in the culture medium were also quantified by ELISA, and the antigen-specific suppression were likewise observed (Supplementary Fig. 20b,c). To directly detect antigen-specific Treg cells, I-Aᵇ OVA 323-339 tetramer was used. Because OT-II CD4⁺ T cells are inherently OVA reactive and exhibit robust baseline tetramer staining even without treatment, the assay was performed in DBA/1 mice. Upon OVA restimulation, OVA-RM@aCD4Tn pretreatment led to an obvious increase in I-Aᵇ OVA 323-339 tetramer⁺ Treg cells compared to free OVA (G1 vs G2, P=0.0027), whereas CII or CII-RM@aCD4Tn pretreatment failed to induce OVA-specific Treg cells (Supplementary Fig. 20d).

Moreover, the functional properties of CII-specific Treg cells were investigated (Supplementary Fig. 21a). CII-specific Treg cells markedly suppressed CII-induced BMDC activation, as evidenced by reduced CD80 and CD86 expression and decreased TNF, together with increased TGF-β levels in the supernatant (G3 vs G5, all P<0.0001) (Fig. 3i and Supplementary Fig. 21b). In contrast, OVA-specific Treg cells exerted only modest effects under the same CII restimulation conditions (Fig. 3i and Supplementary Fig. 21b). Following co-culture, Treg cells from both groups (G4 and G5) showed upregulation of CTLA4 (OVA-specific Treg cells with P=0.0002, CII-specific Treg cells with P<0.0001) and LAG-3 (both P<0.0001) expression compared to unstimulated states, and CTLA4 and LAG-3 expression in CII-specific Treg cells were 1.7-fold and 1.3-fold higher than in OVA-specific Treg cells (Supplementary Fig. 21c), suggesting their greater immunosuppressive activity. Collectively, these data demonstrate that Treg cells induced by Ag-RM@aCD4Tn confer antigen-specific immune tolerance that is engaged upon re-encounter with the cognate antigen.

To further elucidate the immunosuppressive mechanism mediated by OVA-RM@aCD4Tn, we performed transcriptomic analysis on CD4+ T cells isolated from the LNs of OT-II mice 4 days post-administration. Principal components analysis (PCA) revealed a high degree of similarity in gene expression profiles between OVA-RM@Tn and OVA-RM@aCD4Tn groups (Supplementary Fig. 22a). However, the magnitude of gene expression changes in OVA-RM@aCD4Tn group was more pronounced than in OVA-RM@Tn group when compared to OVA group (Supplementary Fig. 22b). In OVA-RM@aCD4Tn-treated mice, the cluster heatmap analysis illustrated a downregulation of pro-inflammatory mediators, including Il6, Tnf, Mmp9, Il1b and Il17a, alongside a upregulation of anti-inflammatory genes such as Il10, Foxp3, Tgfb1, Ctla4 and Il1rn (Fig. 3j), with these regulatory effects being more pronounced than those observed in the OVA-RM@Tn group. Gene ontology (GO) analysis of differentially expressed genes revealed enrichment of biological processes related to immune regulation and inflammatory response after OVA-RM@aCD4Tn intervention (Fig. 3k). Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway enrichment further supported modulation of immune-related signaling, such as TGF-β, T cell receptor and TNF pathways (Supplementary Fig. 23). Taken together, OVA-RM@aCD4Tn exerted enhanced immunomodulatory program compared to OVA-RM@Tn.

6. Therapeutic and prophylactic efficacy of CII-RM@aCD4Tn in CIA mice
To evaluate the early therapeutic potential of this system, different nanoformulations were administered on day 22, 25 and 28 to treat collagen induced arthritis (CIA) mice (Fig. 4a). At the study endpoint, arthritis severity was assessed via blinded scoring of paw swelling and redness. Mice treated with CII-RM@aCD4Tn exhibited significantly reduced arthritis severity, with arthritis scores decreasing from 12.2 in PBS group to 1 (P<0.0001) (Fig. 4b), indicating substantial alleviation of joint inflammation and edema. When aCD4 was absent from the NV surface (G6), arthritis scores upgraded from 1 to 4.3 (P=0.0074) (Fig. 4b), consistent with an important contribution of DC-CD4 bridging by CII-RM@aCD4Tn. Additionally, whereas PBS group experienced pronounced body weight loss due to disease progression and severe swelling34, this effect was greatly attenuated in CII-RM@aCD4Tn-treated mice, which prevented 86.7% of the body weight loss observed in PBS group (P<0.0001) (Fig. 4c). Measurement of paw thickness further confirmed that CII-RM@aCD4Tn provided the most effective treatment outcome among all groups (Fig. 4d). We subsequently performed behavioral assessment to evaluate motor coordination and balance using a rotarod system. Mice treated with CII-RM@aCD4Tn showed significant improvements in multiple rotarod performance metrics across two training sessions, including fewer falls from the rotating rod and an increased rotating speed at the time of falling compared to PBS (all P<0.0001) (Fig. 4e).

We next assessed the pathological severity of the ankle joint through histological analysis. Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained sections of ankle joints from CII-RM@aCD4Tn-treated mice revealed nearly restored joint architecture, with a well-defined articular cavity and minimal synovitis or cartilage degeneration (Fig. 4f,g). In contrast, the PBS group showed severe pathological changes, including extensive inflammatory cell infiltration, synovial hyperplasia, pannus formation, and cartilage erosion (Fig. 4f,g). Pannus formation in the synovial intimal lining is a characteristic of the pathological feature of RA35. In immunohistochemical-stained sections, CII-RM@aCD4Tn-treated mice demonstrated the smallest IL-6 positive area in the joint and synovium among all groups, corresponding to a 76.8% reduction compared to PBS group (P<0.0001) (Fig. 4h,i). Masson staining revealed widespread synovial fibrosis in PBS group, whereas the CII-RM@aCD4Tn-treated group exhibited only 12.0% fibrosis area, representing a 94.2% reduction compared to PBS group (Fig. 4j,k). Moreover, Safranin O-Fast Green (SO-FG) staining revealed well-preserved cartilage architecture in CII-RM@aCD4Tn-treated group, with cartilage thickness of 135.5 μm, closely resembling that of healthy group (P>0.9999) (Fig. 4l,m). Since bone erosion is one of the key accountings for disease severity and poor prognosis36, three-dimensional micro-CT imaging was employed to evaluate bone integrity. The bone structures of ankle in PBS group displayed severe bone erosion, rough bone surfaces, and trabecular bone damage in tibia, fibula, and astragalus (Fig. 4n-p and Supplementary Fig. 24). In contrast, CII-RM@aCD4Tn-treated group presented improved bone structure, as reflected by significant improved micro-CT parameters in quantitative analysis of the region of interest (ROI) (G2 vs G7, all P<0.0001) (Fig. 4n-p and Supplementary Fig. 24), suggesting effective protection of bone damage. Overall, these results confirm that CII-RM@aCD4Tn effective alleviate inflammation, cartilage degradation, synovial fibrosis, and bone erosion in CIA mice model, demonstrating its therapeutic efficacy in mitigating RA progression and improving joint function.

RA is pathologically characterized by the infiltration of activated T cells and macrophages into the synovial membrane of multiple joints, where they secrete pro-inflammatory cytokines, including IFN-γ, IL-6, IL-1β and TNF37, 38. These cytokines perpetuate the inflammatory cascades, leading to synovial hyperplasia and subsequent bone erosion. Conversely, immunomodulatory cells, particularly Treg cells, help maintain immune homeostasis by secreting anti-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-10 and TGF-β15, 38. Immunofluorescence analysis revealed a marked increase in the proportion of Foxp3+ Treg cells in the synovium after CII-RM@aCD4Tn treatment (Fig. 5a-c). Moreover, Treg populations in LNs and spleen were further explored using FC analysis. Consistently, CII-RM@aCD4Tn markedly expanded the Treg cell population, with Treg cell numbers increasing 9.7-fold in LNs and 4.7-fold in spleen compared to PBS (Fig. 5d-g and Supplementary Fig. 25), indicating a systemic immunomodulatory effect. At the same time, levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-1β, TNF and IFN-γ) were significantly reduced in both serum and synovium (G2 vs G7, all P≤0.0001), while secretion of IL-10 and TGF-β was markedly upregulated (G2 vs G7, all P<0.0001) (Fig. 5h,i and Supplementary Fig. 26). These results suggest that CII-RM@aCD4Tn reprograms the inflammatory microenvironment towards an immunoregulatory state by promoting Treg cell generation and reducing proinflammatory cytokine levels, thereby helping to restore systemic immune homeostasis.

To assess late-phase therapeutic efficacy in CIA model, CII-RM@Tn or CII-RM@aCD4Tn were administered on day 27, 30 and 33, after mice had developed evident paw swelling and redness (Supplementary Fig. 27a). In line with the early-treatment findings, CII-RM@aCD4Tn treatment significantly alleviated arthritis score (P=0.0001), preserved body weight decline (P<0.0001), reduced paw swelling (P<0.0001) and improved motor ability (except for the numbers of falls in first training with P=0.0006, all others P<0.0001) compared to PBS group (Supplementary Fig. 27b-e). In the meanwhile, treatment with CII-RM@aCD4Tn also improved the system immune environment through decreasing pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-1β, TNF and IFN-γ) and increasing anti-inflammatory cytokines (IL-10 and TGF-β) in both serum and synovium (Supplementary Fig. 27f,g), and promoting the expansion of Treg cell populations in LNs and spleen (Supplementary Fig. 27h-k).

In order to investigate the preventive efficacy of CII-RM@aCD4Tn, mice received injections three and two weeks prior to CIA induction (Supplementary Fig. 28a), representing a preconditioning setting that is intrinsically more favorable than treatment of fully established disease. Following CII-RM@aCD4Tn treatment, mice illustrated normal morphology of paws without signs of redness or swelling, and their body weight recovered nearly to healthy levels (Supplementary Fig. 28b-d). Moreover, mice in CII-RM@aCD4Tn group demonstrated the highest motor ability among all treated groups (Supplementary Fig. 28e), indicating preserved joint function. Pro-inflammatory cytokines in CII-RM@aCD4Tn-treated mice decreased to healthy levels, accompanied by an increase in anti-inflammatory cytokines compared to PBS group (Supplementary Fig. 28f). In addition, both the numbers and proportions of Treg cells in LNs and spleen were the highest among all experimental groups (Supplementary Fig. 28g-j). These results highlight the prophylactic potential of the DC-CD4 bridging system in preventing RA progression, underscoring its feasibility as a vaccine-based immunomodulatory strategy.

7. Mechanistic validation and durable efficacy of CII-RM@aCD4Tn
To further clarify the underlying therapeutic mechanism of CII-RM@aCD4Tn, CIA mice were treated with different formulations (Fig. 6a). Free CII (G3) or free RM (G4) failed to control arthritis progression (Fig. 6a-f and Supplementary Fig. 29). To assess antigen specificity, we included an antigen-nonspecific group, OVA-RM@aCD4Tn (G7). OVA-RM@aCD4Tn showed markedly reduced therapeutic efficacy compared to CII-RM@aCD4Tn, as reflected by higher arthritis scores (P=0.0003) and synovitis scores (P<0.0001), and its overall performance was comparable to that of RM@aCD4Tn (G5) (Fig. 6a-f and Supplementary Fig. 29). When CII was administrated separately together with RM@aCD4Tn (G8), the efficacy remained inferior to that of co-loaded CII-RM@aCD4Tn (Fig. 6a-f and Supplementary Fig. 29), suggesting that simply co-injecting of free antigen with NVs is insufficient to induce strong antigen-specific tolerance. Furthermore, to dissect the functional contribution of CTLA4-mediated DC targeting, CTLA4 blocked NV formulation by neutralizing CTLA4 (G6) was prepared. Although this CTLA4 blocked formulation retained partial therapeutic activity, its efficacy was lower than that of CII-RM@aCD4Tn (G9) (Fig. 6a-f and Supplementary Fig. 29). Indeed, RM@aCD4Tn (G5), CII-RM@aCD4Tn lacking CTLA4 (G6), OVA-RM@aCD4Tn (G7), and CII + RM@aCD4Tn (G8) all exhibited significant therapeutic benefit compared to PBS (Fig. 6a-f and Supplementary Fig. 29).

Because non-intravenous routes such as i.d. injection are associated with an increased risk of anti-drug antibody (ADA) formation39-41, we next quantified serum anti-CII IgG levels by ELISA after three i.d. doses. Free CII elicited a robust humoral response, leading to markedly elevated anti-CII IgG titers (G3 vs G2, P<0.0001; G8 vs G2, P=0.0006) (Fig. 6g). In contrast, when CII was delivered in NV form, the antibody response was substantially attenuated (G6 vs G3, P<0.0001; G9 vs G3, P<0.0001) (Fig. 6g), indicating that NV encapsulation limits systemic immunogenicity.

In order to validate the therapeutic durability of CII-RM@aCD4Tn, a re-challenge study was investigated in CIA mice (Fig. 6h). Even without additional treatment (G3 and G4), mice previously treated with CII-RM@aCD4Tn maintained better disease control than those had received CII-RM@Tn, in which arthritis score increased from 3.7 (day 42) to 7.2 (day 57) (Fig. 6i). Upon redosing on day 43 (G5 and G6), CII-RM@aCD4Tn group conferred the greatest therapeutic benefit, with arthritis score reduced to 1.5, and CII-RM@Tn group displayed a partial improvement, with arthritis score decreasing from 7.2 to 5.0 (Fig. 6i). Changes in paw thickness, behavioral assessments and H&E staining of ankle joints demonstrated consistent trends with the arthritis score (Fig. 6j-m), further supporting the sustained efficacy of CII-RM@aCD4Tn in re-challenge CIA model.

8. Essential role of Foxp3⁺ Treg cells in CII-RM@aCD4Tn-mediated protection against CIA
To evaluate whether CII-RM@aCD4Tn induces a sustained endogenous regulatory response capable of suppressing disease pathogenesis, recipient mice were pretreated twice on day -14 and -21 before receiving arthritogenic cell transfer (Fig. 7a). Prophylactic administration of CII-RM@aCD4Tn largely prevented disease, whereas CII-RM@Tn conferred only moderate effects in attenuating arthritis score (P=0.0098) and paw thickness (P=0.1073), improving motor function (number of falls with P=0.0059; speed at falls with P=0.0205), and limiting bone erosion (P=0.0028) compared to CII-RM@aCD4Tn (Fig. 7b-e and Supplementary Fig. 30a). Histological analysis of ankle joints further confirmed the protective effects of CII-RM@aCD4Tn in this model (Fig. 7f,g and Supplementary Fig. 30b,c). In parallel, systemic immune modulation was improved following CII-RM@aCD4Tn treatment (Fig. 7h).

To investigate the role of Foxp3+ Treg cells in the immunomodulatory mechanism of CII-RM@aCD4Tn, we employed Foxp3+ Treg cell deficient mice as recipients. Following arthritogenic cell transfer, mice preconditioned with CII-RM@aCD4Tn exhibited only limited therapeutic benefit compared to PBS treated mice, with no significant difference compared to CII-RM@Tn groups (all P>0.05) (Fig. 8i-k and Supplementary Fig. 31). These findings collectively indicate that treatment with CII-RM@aCD4Tn induces a durable regulatory response mediated by Foxp3+ Treg cells that can restrain pathogenesis driven by the transferred arthritogenic cells.

To directly test whether Treg cells induced by CII-RM@aCD4Tn are responsible for its therapeutic efficacy, we performed adoptive Treg cells transfer in CIA mice (Fig. 7l). CD4+ CD25+ T cells that include Treg cells were isolated from the LNs and spleen of mice treated with i.d. injections of CII-RM@Tn or CII-RM@aCD4Tn. Cells were sorted based on CD4⁺ CD25⁺ expression alone, without Foxp3⁺ selection, to preserve therapeutic activity, as Foxp3⁺ cell sorting requires membrane permeabilization, which compromises viability and precludes successful adoptive transfer6, 42. When donor cells were derived from normal mice, CD4+ CD25+ T cells derived from CII-RM@aCD4Tn-treated mice could significantly lower arthritis score (P=0.0006) and paw thickness (P=0.0201) and improve motor ability (number of falls with P=0.0014; speed at falls with P=0.0189) compared to CII-RM@Tn-treated group (Fig. 7m,n and Supplementary Fig. 32a). Moreover, these mice exhibited increased numbers and proportions of Treg cells in both LNs and spleen (G2 vs G7, all P<0.0001) (Fig. 7o,p and Supplementary Fig. 32b,c), contributing to immune environment remodeling (Fig. 7q).

To further assess the role of CII-RM@aCD4Tn-mediated Foxp3+ Treg cells, Foxp3+ Treg cell deficient mice were used as donor mice. When adoptive Treg cells from Foxp3+ Treg cell deficient mice which were subjected to CII-RM@aCD4Tn, the therapeutic efficacy against RA was declined, producing effects similar to those observed in CII-RM@Tn group (all P>0.05) (Fig. 7r-t and Supplementary Fig. 33). These data suggest that CD4+ CD25+ Foxp3+ Treg cells induced by CII-RM@aCD4Tn are critical mediators of its immunomodulatory effects.

Induction of CD4+ T cells into iCD4 in vitro
CD4+ T cells were isolated from the spleen and lymph nodes (LN) of mice via magnetic bead based negative separation. Briefly, the inguinal, axillary, and mesenteric LNs, along with the spleen were collected from CO2 euthanized mice. Obtained organs were mechanically dissociated through a 70 μm strainer, and the resulting cell suspensions were centrifuged at 4℃, 600 g for 5 min. After removing red blood cells (RBC) with ACK lysis buffer at room temperature (RT) for 3 min, the remaining cells were purified using the EasySep Mouse CD4+ T Cell Isolation Kit according to the manufacturer’s protocol.

Isolated CD4+ T cells were seeded in 6-well plates and activated with plate-bound antibodies against CD3 (1 μg ml-1) and CD28 (2 μg ml-1) in T cell culture medium, which was RPMI 1640 medium supplemented with 10 % (v/v) fetal bovine serum (FBS), 1% (v/v) penicillin/streptomycin, 2 mM L-glutamine, 20 ng ml-1 IL-2 and 20 ng ml-1 IL-7. For iCD4 differentiation, TGF-β (2-20 ng ml-1) and RM (50 nM) were added59, 60. Cells were cultured for 4 days, and iCD4 induction was verified by FC (Aria IIEI, BD) to detect CD25, Foxp3, CTLA4, LAG-3, and PD-1.

Preparation and characterization of Te and Tn
Extracellular vesicles derived from iCD4 were designated as Te. In brief, induced iCD4 were cultured in 1640 medium containing 10% (v/v) exosome-free FBS and 1% (v/v) penicillin/streptomycin for 24 h. The supernatant was collected and centrifuged at 4℃, 500 g for 10 min to remove debris, followed by another centrifugation at 4℃, 3,000 g for 15 min. Te were pelleted by ultracentrifugation (OPTIMAL-90K, BECKMAN) at 4℃, 100,000 g for 2 h.

Nanovesicles (NV) derived from iCD4 were referred to as Tn. Differentiated iCD4 were centrifuged, washed three times with PBS, and then resuspended in PBS at 1 × 107 cells per milliliter. The suspensions were sequentially extruded through polycarbonate membranes with pore sizes of 5 μm, 1 μm, 400 nm and 200 nm via a liposome extruder (LF-1, Avestin), with 20 reciprocal passes for each pore size. The resulting NV suspensions were collected by ultracentrifugation at 4℃, 100,000 g for 2 h.

Te and Tn were quantified using the BCA Protein Assay Kit. To compare their LN targeting ability, Te and Tn with an equivalent amount of protein were labelled with DiR by co-incubation at 37℃ for 30 min, followed by intradermal (i.d.) injection into both flanks of DBA/1 mice. After 24 h, axillary lymph nodes (aLN) and inguinal lymph nodes (iLN) were isolated for fluorescent intensity (FI) detection by an IVIS imaging system (Lumina Series III, PerkinElmer). In addition, when Te or Tn were derived from an equal number of iCD4, LN targeting was also investigated by the same approach.

Preparation of CII-RM@Tn and CII-RM@aCD4Tn
To obtain CII-RM@Tn, iCD4 at a concentration of 1 × 107 cells per milliliter were mixed with CII (20 μg ml-1) and RM (4 μg ml-1), followed by sequential extrusion using the same protocol as for Tn preparation.

Anti-CD4 Fab fragment (aCD4) engineered CII-RM@aCD4Tn were constructed using a DSPE-PEG platform, which avidly inserts into the NV membranes as its hydrophobic segment61, 62. First, DSPE-PEG2000-aCD4 (DP-aCD4) was synthesized by reacting DP-NHS with aCD4 at various molar ratios of 0:1, 2:1, 4:1, 8:1, 12:1, 16:1 and 20:1, and the pH of the solution was adjusted to 8.5 by 1M NaHCO3. The reaction proceeded on a four-dimensional rotator at RT for 12 h, and the products were purified using 50 kDa ultrafiltration tube to remove unconjugated DP-NHS. Next, to shield CD4 protein on the surface of iCD4, the cells were preincubated with free aCD4 (30 μg per million T cells), and then exposed to DP-aCD4 (50 μg per million T cells) at 37℃ for 30 min. Free aCD4 and DP-aCD4 were removed after centrifugation at 4℃, 600 g for 5 min to collect aCD4 modified iCD4 (aCD4-iCD4). Finally, CII-RM@aCD4Tn were produced by sequential extrusion following the same steps as CII-RM@Tn.

Characterization of CII-RM@aCD4Tn
Protein profiles of iCD4 and Tn were analyzed using 10% SDS-PAGE followed by Coomassie blue staining. To evaluate the anchoring efficiency of DP-aCD4 to CD4+ T cells, Cy3-labelled aCD4 with varying DP molar modification ratios were incubated with CD4+ T cells at 37℃ for 30 min. After centrifugation, the FI of the supernatant was detected by a Microplate reader (CLARIOstar Plus, BMG LABTECH) to calculate the amount of DP-aCD4 inserted into the cell membrane. Cy3-labelled CII-RM@aCD4Tn were incubated with CD4+ T cells at 37℃ for 30 min, followed by FC detection to calculate the conjugation ability. Cy3-labelled CII-RM@Tn or CII-RM@aCD4Tn were incubated with CD4+ T cells for confocal imaging (AX R, Nikon). FITC-labelled RM, Cy3-labelled collagen, and Cy5-labelled aCD4 were employed to fabricate CII-RM@aCD4Tn, followed by confocal detection. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) was used to assess the morphology of Tn, aCD4Tn, CII-RM@Tn, and CII-RM@aCD4Tn. A particle size analyzer (Zetasizer Lab, Malvern) was employed to measure the hydrodynamic size and zeta potential.

Various feeding ratios of CII (5, 10, 15, 20 μg ml-1) and RM (1, 2, 3, 4 μg ml-1) were tested when synthesizing CII-RM@aCD4Tn. Encapsulation efficiencies and loading capacities of CII were determined by Collagen ELISA kit according to the manufacturer’s protocol. RM content was confirmed by HPLC under the following conditions: column temperature 50℃, mobile phase 10 mM ammonium acetate and acetonitrile (25:75, v/v), flow rate 1.5 ml min-1, and injection volume 5 μl. Before measurement, NVs were disrupted with 0.1% Triton X-100 for 10 min. Drug release profiles were evaluated by dialyzing the samples in dialysis bags (MW cutoff 800 kDa) against PBS at 37℃, with aliquots of the external solution collected over 24 h for quantification.

NVs stability was first examined by measuring the particle size of Tn, aCD4Tn, CII-RM@Tn and CII-RM@aCD4Tn in PBS or 10% FBS at 4℃ over a week. To investigate storage stability, CII-RM@aCD4Tn were maintained at -80, -20, 4 and 25℃ for 0, 7, 14 and 21 days, followed by size measurements. The bioactivity of membrane proteins was tested by incubating stored samples with dye-labelled antibodies against CD25, CTLA4, PD-1, and recombinant CD4 at RT for 15 min, then measuring the FI of the supernatant after ultracentrifugation.

The uptake of CII-RM@aCD4Tn by bone marrow-derived dendritic cells (BMDC) was evaluated. BMDCs were generated from male DBA/1 mice by flushing bone marrow from the femur and tibia with PBS. RBCs were removed by ACK lysis buffer and then filtered through a 70 μm cell strainer to remove debris. The collected cells were cultured in RPMI 1640 medium supplemented with 10% (v/v) FBS, 1% (v/v) penicillin-streptomycin, and 20 ng ml-1 GM-CSF to promote differentiation. After 3 days, fresh medium was added. On day 7, BMDCs were harvested and purified using a EasySep Mouse CD11c+ Selection Kit for subsequent experiments.

For NVs uptake and presentation evaluation, CII and RM were labelled with FITC. BMDCs (1 × 106 cells per well in a 6-well plate) were incubated with CII-RM@aCD4Tn or free drug (FITC-CII and FITC-RM) on an orbital shaker at 40 rpm for 12 or 24 h. After that, BMDCs were washed twice with PBS, and stained with DAPI for nuclei and DiI for membrane. Before confocal observation, cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) and resuspended in antifade mounting medium. To detect the Eα peptide on MHC II of BMDCs, free Eα plus RM or Eα-RM@aCD4Tn treated BMDCs for 24 h were stained with dye-labelled I-Ab monoclonal antibody, DAPI and DiI for confocal imaging.

Immunosuppression of CII-RM@aCD4Tn on DC and CD4+ T cells
To examine tolerogenic DCs (tDC), BMDCs were co-cultured with different NVs for 48 h and then activated with LPS (50 ng ml-1) for an additional 24 h. tDCs were induced by adding 10 ng ml-1 IL-10 and 10 ng ml-1 TGF-β into the medium for 72 h. Afterward, the expression levels of CD80, CD86, MHC II, CD40 and PD-L1 were detected by FC. The mRNA levels of TNF and TGF-β in the cells were evaluated with the qRT-PCR StepOnePlus Real-Time PCR system (Applied Biosystems, CA). The primers used for mRNA level analysis were listed in Supplementary table 2. In parallel, ELISA was conducted to measure the secretion levels of TNF and TGF-β from BMDCs.

For iCD4 analysis, CD4⁺ T cells were co-cultured with each NVs type for 48 h and stimulated with PMA (20 ng ml-1) for 6 h. Positive iCD4 were induced by supplying with 10 ng ml-1 IL-10 and 10 ng ml-1 TGF-β for 72 h. FC was used to detect CTLA4, CD127 and PD-1 expression, while qRT-PCR and ELISA were performed to measure TNF and TGF-β in cells and culture supernatants, respectively.

Bridging effect of CII-RM@aCD4Tn on CD4+ T cells and DCs
The DC-CD4 bridging ability of CII-RM@aCD4Tn was assessed by co-incubating BMDCs (1 × 106) and CD4⁺ T cells (1 × 106) with either CII-RM@Tn or CII-RM@aCD4Tn at 37 ℃ for 1 h. Cells were then fixed at RT for 30 min, and stained with dye-labelled antibodies against CD4 and CD11c to detect DC-CD4 cell pairs via FC.

To visualize DC-CD4 engagement of CII-RM@aCD4Tn in vivo, Cy5-labelled CII-RM@aCD4Tn were administered i.d. into male DBA/1 mice at both flanks. Mice were CO2 euthanized 24 h later, iLNs were harvested for cryosection, followed by staining with dye-labelled CD11c and CD4 antibodies. These sections were subjected to panoramic scanning (Pannoramic MID-250FLASH-DESK, 3DHISTECH). To precisely identify the cell populations targeted by NVs, iLNs were mechanically dissociated into single cell suspensions and then analyzed by FC for CD4, CD11c, CD11b, Ly6G and CD19.

To assess the contribution of different APC subsets to iCD4 induction, CD11c+ DCs, CD11b⁺ macrophages, Ly6G⁺ neutrophils and CD19⁺ B cells derived from male DBA/1 mice were co-cultured with CD4+ T cells (1 × 106) at a number ratio of 1:1 in the presence of CII-RM@aCD4Tn for 3 days. IL-10 levels in culture medium were quantified by ELISA.

To investigate the interaction mechanism between CII-RM@aCD4Tn and DCs, BMDCs were preincubated with CTLA4 Ig to block surface CD80/86, and CII-RM@aCD4Tn was pretreated with an anti-CTLA4 antibody to mask CTLA4 on the surface of NV. DC-CD4 cell pairs were then quantified by FC.

Biodistribution of CII-RM@aCD4Tn
Cy5-labelled CII-RM@aCD4Tn were injected i.d. into male DBA/1 mice either at one flank or both flanks with the same total dosage. Mice were CO2 euthanized 12 h later, and the heart, liver, spleen, lung, kidney, aLNs and iLNs were harvested for IVIS imaging. To track in vivo release, Cy5-labelled CII plus RM or CII-RM@aCD4Tn were injected i.d. at the right flank of male DBA/1 mice. The FI at the injected site was monitored for up to 7 days by IVIS. Concurrently, the FI in the ipsilateral iLN was monitored for up to 13 days

Safety evaluation of CII-RM@aCD4
For in vivo safety assessment, male DBA/1 mice were randomly assigned to six groups, and each group contained 6 mice. One group was healthy (G1), whereas the other five groups included 150 μg CII + 20 μg RM (G3), 1 mg Tn (G4), 1mg aCD4Tn (G5), 1.2 mg CII-RM@Tn (G6) and 1.2 mg CII-RM@aCD4Tn (G7). Each formulation was injected i.d. on both flanks of mice on day 0 and 3. On day 7, blood was collected from mice in each group for liver function tests and complete blood counts. After CO2 euthanizing mice, the heart, liver, spleen, lung and kidney were harvested, and analyzed by H&E staining to detect any pathological abnormalities.

Antigen-specific T cell induction in vitro and in vivo
Treg cell induction was initially explored in vitro by incubating various NVs with splenocytes. Briefly, splenocytes were harvested from OT-II transgenic mice, in which CD4+ T cells specifically respond to chicken OVA peptide. Therefore, OVA was used as the antigen to fabricate OVA-RM@Tn or OVA-RM@aCD4Tn. Splenocytes were suspended in T cell culture medium and plated in 6-well plates coated with CD3 (1 μg ml-1) and CD28 (2 μg ml-1) antibodies. Different NVs were added for co-incubation for 72 h, followed by OVA (50 μg ml-1) activation for 24 h. After that, cells were collected, and then analyzed by FC for CD45, CD4, CD25 and Foxp3. The levels of TNF and TGF-β in the medium were also quantified by ELISA.

For in vivo Treg cell induction, OVA encapsulated NVs were injected i.d. at both flanks of OT-II mice. Four days later, aLNs, iLNs and spleen were harvested for Treg cell analysis using FC after adding 2 μl counting beads and staining for CD45, CD4, CD25 and Foxp3. For Treg cell induction in wild-type mice, male DBA/1 mice received two i.d. injections of CII loaded NVs at weekly intervals. Seven days after the second dose, mice were immunized i.d. on both sides of the flank with a CII emulsion, prepared by homogenizing CII and CFA at 1:1 volume under ice-cold condition. After one week, aLNs, iLNs and spleen were collected for Treg cell analysis.

To assess antigen-specific tolerance, OT-II and DBA/1 mice were injected i.d. at both flanks with OVA or CII encapsulated NVs. After that, splenocytes were harvested for IFN-γ ELISPOT assays to evaluate the specific activation. Splenocytes were seeded into ELISPOT plates with 1 × 106 cells per well, and stimulated with 10 μg ml-1 OVA or 10 μg ml-1 CII respectively. After 24 h, supernatants were collected for TNF and TGF-β detection by using ELISA kits, and IFN-γ-secreting cells were quantified according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Furthermore, OVA-specific Treg cells in splenocytes from DBA/1 mice were analyzed by staining with I-Ab OVA 323-339 Tetramer.

For functional characterization of CII-specific Treg cells, DBA/1 mice were treated as described above, and CD4⁺ CD25⁺ T cells were isolated and cocultured with BMDCs in the presence of 50 ng ml-1 LPS and 10 μg ml-1 CII. After 24 h, culture supernatants were collected for the measurement of TNF and TGF-β levels, and CD80/CD86 expression on BMDCs and CTLA4 and LAG-3 on Treg cells were analyzed by FC.

RNA sequencing and differential gene enrichment analysis
OVA, OVA-RM@Tn or OVA-RM@aCD4Tn was injected i.d. into both flanks of OT-II mice. After 4 days, CD4+ T cells were isolated from iLNs and aLNs. Total RNA was extracted from the collected CD4+ T cells according to the manufacturer’s instructions. RNA libraries were constructed and pooled based on their effective concentrations. High-quality sequencing data were quantified at the transcript level using HTSeq. RNA sequencing was performed on the MGISEQ-T7 platform, and subsequent bioinformatic analyses were conducted using the online platform (https://www.bioinformatics.com.cn/).

Therapeutics efficacy of CII-RM@aCD4Tn in CIA mice
To establish the collagen induced arthritis (CIA) mouse model, male DBA/1 mice were injected i.d. with 100 μl CII emulsion (CII:CFA=1:1) at the tail base of both sides, followed 21 days later by a boost immunization with CII in IFA. Mice were randomly divided into seven groups, and each group contained 6 mice. One group served as a healthy (G1), whereas the other six groups included PBS (G2), 150 μg CII + 20 μg RM (G3), 1 mg Tn (G4), 1 mg aCD4Tn (G5), 1.2 mg CII-RM@Tn (G6) and 1.2 mg CII-RM@aCD4Tn (G7). Notably, the amounts of CII and RM delivered in G6 and G7 were equivalent to those in G3. Early therapeutic intervention was performed from day 22 to 28 (three injections total, every three days) by i.d. injection at both flanks, and the injected dose was 200 μl per mouse. For late treatment, mice exhibiting paw swelling at day 27 were administered three doses of CII-RM@Tn (G6) or CII-RM@aCD4Tn (G7) every three days from day 27 to 33.

Arthritis score and body weight were recorded every three days. Arthritis score was evaluated according to the following criteria: 0, no evidence of erythema and swelling; 1, erythema and mild swelling confined to the tarsals or ankle joint; 2, erythema and mild swelling extending from the ankle to the tarsals; 3, erythema and moderate swelling extending from the ankle to metatarsal joints; 4, erythema and severe swelling encompassing the ankle, foot and digits, or ankylosis of the limb. Each paw was scored individually, and the maximum score was 16 for each mouse63. On day 42, paw thickness was measured, and rotarod test was conducted. Serum and synovium levels of IL-6, IL-1β, TNF, IFN-γ, IL-10 and TGF-β were quantified using ELISA kits. The count and percentage of Treg cells in spleens and LNs were determined by FC.

Rotarod test
A computerized rotarod apparatus (ZL-200c, Bestcell) was used to assess motor coordination. Mice were initially habituated to the experimental setup by placing them on the stationary rod for a period of 2~3 min daily for two consecutive days, to minimize stress and ensure familiarity with the apparatus. On day 41, mice were placed on the rotating rod at a constant speed of 15 rpm for 3 min, and the number of times they fell off the rod was recorded. Additionally, the speed of rotation was gradually increased from 4 to 20 rpm over 3 min, and the rotating speed was recorded when mice fell. This procedure was repeated on day 42.

Histological and immunohistochemical analysis of inflamed joints
To evaluate RA-related pathological changes, including angiogenesis, synovitis, cartilage destruction and fibrosis, hind ankle joints were harvested at the endpoint and subjected to hematoxylin and eosin (H&E), safranin O-fast green (SO-FG), and Masson staining. H&E sections were scored by three pathologists according to three features of chronic synovitis: enlargement of lining cell layer, cellular density of synovial stroma and leukocytic infiltration. Each feature was semi-quantitatively evaluated on a scale from 0 (absent) to 3 (strong). The sum of these yielded the synovitis score, which was interpreted as follows: 0~1, no synovitis; 2~4, low-grade synovitis; 5~9, high-grade synovitis64. Cartilage thickness in the tibia and talus was measured in SO-FG sections by Image J software (version 1.53c). Fibrotic areas of synovium in Masson sections were quantified by Image J software.

Microcomputed tomography (micro-CT) (SkyScan 1276, Bruker) scans was performed on hind paws according to the following parameters: source current, 385 μA; source voltage, 65 kV; image pixel size, 17.76 µm; vertical object position, 109.456 mm; optical axis, 653 line; filter, Al 1 mm. To compare the therapeutic effects of the different groups, three-dimensional images were reconstructed using Mimics software (Materialize) and the bone volume/total volume (BV/TV), trabecular thickness (Tb. Th), trabecular number (Tb. N), trabecular separation (Tb. Sp), structural model index (SMI), and bone mineral density (BMD) in the tibia were calculated by CTAn software (Skyscan).

Immunohistochemical analysis was also performed to observe the distribution of IL-6 in the synovium of ankle joints, and the IL-6 positive areas was quantified using Image J software. To visualize the distribution of Treg cells in synovium, the hind ankle joints were stained with dye-labelled CD4, CD25 and Foxp3 antibody, followed by Image J software analysis.

Mechanistic investigation of CII-RM@aCD4Tn
CIA mice were established as above method. Mice were randomly divided into nine groups, and each group contained 6 mice. One group served as a healthy (G1), whereas the other eight groups included PBS (G2), 150 μg CII (G3), 20 μg RM (G4), 1 mg RM@aCD4Tn (G5), 1.2 mg CII-RM@aCD4Tn (lacking CTLA4) (G6), 1.2 mg OVA-RM@aCD4Tn (G7), 150 μg CII + 1 mg RM@aCD4Tn (G8) and 1.2 mg CII-RM@aCD4Tn (G9). The amounts of CII and RM were identical across all groups. Notably, CTLA4 on the surface of Tn was blocked via anti-CTLA4 antibody to generate group 6. The NVs were injected on day 22, 25 and 28. Arthritis score and body weight were monitored every three days. Paw thickness measurement and rotarod test were conducted on day 42. Hind paws were collected for H&E staining. In addition, serum samples were obtained on day 42 for quantification of anti-CII IgG antibodies using an ELISA kit.

Re-challenge study of CII-RM@aCD4Tn in CIA mice
To investigate therapeutic durability, DBA/1 mice that had completed the initial three-dose treatment were re-challenged with CII antigen on day 42. Male DBA/1 mice were randomly assigned to six groups, and each group contained 6 mice. One group was healthy (G1), while the other five groups included PBS (G2), 1.2 mg CII-RM@Tn (G3), 1.2 mg CII-RM@aCD4Tn (G4), 1.2 mg CII-RM@Tn with redose (G5) and 1.2 mg CII-RM@aCD4Tn with redose (G6). Each dose of CII-RM@Tn or CII-RM@aCD4Tn contained 150 μg CII and 20 μg RM. On day 42, 100 μl CII emulsion (CII:IFA=1:1) was injected i.d. at both sides of the tail base. On day 43, mice in groups G5 and G6 received a single additional (redose) injection of the corresponding formulation. Arthritis scores and body weight were monitored every three days. Paw thickness and motor performance (rotarod test) were assessed on day 57, and hind paws were collected for histological analysis by H&E staining.

Prophylactic efficacy of CII-RM@aCD4Tn in CIA mice
To assess prophylactic potential, DBA/1 mice were administered NVs prior to CIA induction. Male DBA/1 mice were randomly assigned to seven groups, and each group contained 6 mice. One group was healthy (G1), while the other six groups included PBS (G2), 150 μg CII + 20 μg RM (G3), 1 mg Tn (G4), 1mg aCD4Tn (G5), 1.2 mg CII-RM@Tn (G6) and 1.2 mg CII-RM@aCD4Tn (G7). The amounts of CII and RM delivered in G6 and G7 were equivalent to those in G3. The NVs were injected twice on day -21 and day -14, followed by CIA induction on day 0 and day 21. Arthritis score and body weight were monitored every three days. Paw thickness measurement and rotarod test were conducted on day 42. The levels of IL-6, IL-1β, TNF, IFN-γ, IL-10 and TGF-β in serum and synovium were examined using ELISA kits. The numbers and percentage of Treg cells in spleen and LNs were detected by FC.

Adoptive transfer of arthritogenic cells
CIA model was established in female C57BL/6 mice through two rounds of collagen immunization, which was similar to that in male DBA/1. After 6 days of second immunization, splenocytes were collected and suspended in T cell culture medium. These cells were seeded in plates which were bound with CD3 (1 μg ml-1) and CD28 (2 μg ml-1) antibodies, and activated with 50 μg ml-1 of CII for 72 h to generate arthritogenic cells. Recipient mice received PBS, CII-RM@Tn or CII-RM@aCD4Tn on days -21 and -14 before accepting an i.v. injection of 2 × 10⁷ arthritogenic cells. Each group included 6 mice. Arthritis score, paw thickness and rotarod test were conducted. Right hind paws were collected for micro-CT and H&E, SO-FG and Masson section staining. The levels of IL-6, IL-1β, TNF, IFN-γ, IL-10 and TGF-β in serum and synovium were examined.

To confirm the functional role of Foxp3+ Treg cells, Foxp3-IRES-DTR mice were enrolled as recipient mice, allowing for the specific deletion of Foxp3+ Treg cells in vivo. These mice received 2 μg/kg diphtheria toxin daily by i.v. injection from days -24 to -22, followed by one dose per week until the end time point to ensure complete depletion of Foxp3+ Treg cells. Subsequently, these mice were pretreated with PBS, CII-RM@Tn or CII-RM@aCD4Tn on day -21 and day -14, and then transferred i.v. with 2 × 10⁷ arthritogenic cells. Arthritis score, paw thickness and rotarod test were performed.

Adoptive transfer of regulatory cells
Female C57BL/6 mice were administered i.d. with PBS, CII-RM@Tn or CII-RM@aCD4Tn on day -21 and day -14. Splenocytes were collected 6 days after the second injection, and suspended in T cell culture medium. These cells were stimulated with 50 μg ml-1 CII plus plate-bound anti-CD3 and anti-CD28 for 72 h to generate regulatory cells, and CD4+ CD25+ T cells were isolated using the EasySep Mouse CD4+ CD25+ T Cell Isolation Kit according to the manufacturer’s protocol. After that, 2 × 106 of CD4+ CD25+ T cells were transferred i.v. into recipient mice. One day later, recipient mice underwent CIA induction. Arthritis score, paw thickness and rotarod test were conducted. The levels of IL-6, IL-1β, TNF, IFN-γ, IL-10 and TGF-β in serum and synovium were examined. Treg cells in spleen and LNs were checked by FC.

To confirm the therapeutic role of Foxp3+ Treg cells, Foxp3-IRES-DTR mice were employed as donor mice. These mice were pretreated with PBS, CII-RM@Tn or CII-RM@aCD4Tn on day -21 and -14, and Foxp3+ Treg cells were depleted by three consecutive i.v. injections of 2 μg/kg diphtheria toxin from day -7 to -5. On day -3, splenocytes were harvested and stimulated with 50 μg ml-1 CII for 72 h. After that, isolated CD4+ CD25+ T cells were transferred i.v into recipient mice at 2 × 106 cells per mouse, followed by CIA induction. Arthritis score, paw thickness and rotarod test were performed.

Statistics and reproducibility
All data are presented as means ± SD., and statistical analysis was performed using GraphPad Prism software (version 10.1). Data comparisons were made by unpaired two-tailed t-test, one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with Tukey’s post hoc test or two-way ANOVA with Tukey’s post hoc test. All n values reported represent biologically independent replicates. For experiments presenting representative images, the number of independent repeats with similar results is consistent with the biologically independent replicates used for statistical analysis when quantification is provided; for representative image experiments without statistical analysis, experiments are repeated independently at least three times with similar results.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

In the present manuscript, the authors have detailed the general characteristics and initial functional studies with a regulatory CD4+ T cell (Treg)-based extrusion nanoparticle (NP). The primary premise for utilization of this method is to produce a NP that contains both CTLA4 (to targt CD80/CD86+ dendritic cells (DCs)) and anti-CD4 Fab on the surface of the NP (to target CD4+ T cells), while encapsuling rapamycin and antigen (Ag) within the NP. While the data are extensive for characterization of the NP and there are promising data for the functionality of the NP in vivo, there are critical controls and deficiencies within the data sets which preclude publication.
Comments:
1. In the Abstract the authors imply that the generation of Tregs in vitro for use as a therapeutic is too intricate and that the in vivo induction of Treg in vivo is insufficient for the treatment of autoimmune disease. However, the present methodology first requires the induction and/or expansion of Tregs in vitro, and the goal of this NP therapy is to induce Ag-specific Tregs in vivo. This would appear to be the authors arguing against the translatability of their own therapy. Additionally, Figure 1a presents data showing that the in vitro induction of Tregs is only up to 27% of total T cells. This is an extremely low percentage for in vitro induction cultures. The contour plot presented also indicates that the analysis has compensation issues, as the double-positive FoxP3+/CD25+ population is a thin rocket. This same compensation issue is present in Figure 4b, 6e, and 7h.
2. In the presentation of Tregs within the spleen and the lymph nodes, the authors use different dating for the presented contour plots. Why is this?
3. In the present dosing scheme in vivo, the mice receive 3 doses that are separated by 3 days. While the treatment appears to be promising, do the authors know if mice can be redosed at later dates?
4. Have the authors measured the level of NP-associated Ag antibody production? The injection of NP via the present route of administration is well known to induce significant ADA responses.
5. The authors present data showing that both rapamycin and the loaded Ag are released from the NP within 12-24hrs in vitro. It would also be presumed that NP of the 150-200nm size with a negative surface charge would be phagocytosed by neutrophils and macrophages. As such, have the authors assessed if any other APC population is targeted by their NP?
6. Beside DCs, activated monocyte/macrophages, and B cells will express CD80/CD86. This is particularly a confounder with the present hypothesis of only targeting DCs in the therapeutic setting. As an illustration of this, the data present in Figure 3c show that the vast majority of the CII-RM@aCD4n is not close to the CD11c+ stained cells within the lymph node. Do the authors know what other cell type the CII-RM@aCD4n may be interacting within the lymph nodes post injection?
7. The authors state that bone marrow cells cultured in the presence of GMCSF are DCs. This is incorrect. While there will be a portion of the cells that are DCs, the cultures will be a mixed population of monocytes, macrophages, DCs, and some neutrophils. Did the authors complete any additional selective driving on the cell population or purification of the resultant cell prior to culture in the presence of their NP to support the claim that BMDCs were used in these studies were bonified BMDCs?
8. In Figure 2g and 2h it is stated that CII-RM@aCD4Tn more readily targeted the Ag to cells as compared to free Ag. This is an artifact of the culture system. The BMDCs will be on the bottom of the well, and the free Ag will be even dispersed throughout the volume of the well. In contrast, the NP will also more readily settle to the bottom of the well, where the BMDCs are located. The present comment is not to refute the presented data, but instead the usable conclusion from this experiment is limited due to the model system used.
9. What is the total dosage of rapamycin and Ag given per dose of CII-RM@aCD4Tn?
10. In the disease course data presented in Figures 5 and 7, a critical treatment group is missing. The authors have not included an Ag-non-specific version of Ag-RM@aCD4Tn. Given the authors hypothesis that the use of CTLA4+ NP coated with anti-CD4Fab will specifically pull DCs and CD4+ T cells together, and the data from Supplementary Figure 5b showing that rapamycin is released from the NPs within 12-24hrs, the authors cannot determine if functional decrease in disease severity is truly Ag-specific or if this effect is merely due to more targeted release of rapamycin to CD4+ T cells.
11. The authors completed tracking studies to determine the location of the NPs post dosing. Beside the draining lymph node, the data show that a significant amount of the NP-associated signal is present within the liver. Have the authors assessed T cell populations within this organ post dosing, as the liver is also held to be a tolerogenic site.
12. Can the injection of exogenous Ag mixed with RM@aCD4Tn induce the same response as CII- RM@aCD4Tn? Meaning, does the Ag and NP need to be connected locationally for the functional activity? This would be critical for an in vivo setting; this is important given the Ag-release profile of RM@aCD4Tn (Supplementary Figure 5b) and the argument that Ag-specific tolerance is induced.
13. The authors state that Ag-specific tolerance is induced, but the data used to support this claim are from OTII mice treated with OVA-RM@aCD4Tn and the ex vivo recall cultures compare the OVA ex vivo recall response to the CII ex vivo recall response. As the OTII T cell are TCR transgenic and cannot respond to CII in the absence or presence of OVA-RM@aCD4Tn, this in no way shows that OVA-RM@aCD4Tn treatment is Ag-specific.
14. On line 288, the authors state that CII-RM@aCD4Tn induced an increase in Ag-specific Tregs. However, the authors did not use tracible TCR transgenic T cells or tetramer staining to support this conclusion. Here again, the authors also did not used an Ag-non-specific RM@aCD4Tn control treatment, as such the authors cannot claim that these cells are Ag-specific Tregs due to the treatment.
15. In Figure 5a-c, the author claim that treatments G2-G5 made disease severity worse. However, the authors have not included a saline/PBS treatment group. What treatment group are the authors using as the comparator to make this claim?
16. In Figure 6b and 6c, the percentage of area for FoxP3+ cells is ~0.7%, while the CD4+CD25+FoxP3+ area is ~2%. How is the area increasing by increasing the stringency of marker co-expression for quantifying the cells?
17. Figure 1b presents a summary of the hypothesis. This should be either removed or placed at the end of the manuscript as part of the Discussion. With the present placement of the figure, this is attempting to lead the reader to make the same conclusion as the author without the reader having been able to objectively review the data first.
18. Figure 7 and Extended Data Figure 8 are the same figure.
19. The authors neglect to mention any of the multiple companies and academic laboratories that have Ag-specific therapeutics and Ag-specific NP-based therapeutics that are presently in clinical trials.

### Reviewer 2

This manuscript presents a nanoparticle platform based on Treg cell-derived membrane nanoparticles (Tn) decorated with anti-CD4 (aCD4) antibodies and encapsulated with an antigenic peptide (AP) and rapamycin (RM), designed to induce antigen-specific Tregs for the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis (RA). While the therapeutic potential of the platform is of interest, the manuscript falls short in demonstrating significant advancement over previously published technologies, and the mechanistic claims are not sufficiently supported by the data. Below are specific concerns and suggestions.
1. This study failed to demonstrate advancement over prior work. A closely related study has previously been reported (Science Advances 8(47), eabo5284, 2022), demonstrating that nanoparticles co-loaded with antigenic peptide and rapamycin can effectively induce tolerogenic dendritic cells (tDCs) and antigen-specific Tregs for treatment of arthritis. The principal advancement claimed in the current study is the addition of CTLA-4 and anti-CD4 antibody to the nanoparticle surface. While some positive effects of anti-CD4 are demonstrated in the manusript, the role of CTLA-4 remains speculative due to the absence of proper in vivo controls. To substantiate the contribution of CTLA-4, the authors should include control nanoparticles lacking CTLA-4 but retaining anti-CD4 decoration. Furthermore, the above-mentioned study should be properly cited and discussed in the Introduction to clarify how the current work advances the field.
2. The mechanistic claims were not experimentally supported. Figure 1b proposes that AP-RM@aCD4Tn interacts with CD80/86 on DCs via CTLA-4 to induce immune tolerance and promote tDC formation, mediated by both the surface-bound molecules and release of RM and AP. However, the manuscript lacks direct evidence supporting CTLA-4–CD80/86 interactions. Data presented in Figures 2g and 2h show internalization of Cll-RM@aCD4Tn (AP = collagen II) by DCs but do not address surface-level immunological synapse formation. Additionally, while Figure 1b depicts release of rapamycin from the nanoparticle, no data are presented to confirm this, and prior work (Science Advances 8(47), eabo5284, 2022) indicates that rapamycin is typically retained within lipid layers rather than being readily released. These mechanistic assertions require either experimental support or more cautious interpretation.
3. This study lacks evidence for collagen II-specific Treg induction in vivo. While Figure 6 suggests in vivo Treg induction by Cll-RM@aCD4Tn, the manuscript does not demonstrate that these Tregs are specific to collagen II. This is a critical gap, given that collagen II antigen specificity is central to the therapeutic rationale for RA. The authors are encouraged to perform functional assays to confirm collagen II specificity; e.g., co-culturing isolated Tregs with DCs in the presence of collagen II, followed by proliferation or cytokine profiling assays.
4. This approach concerns feasibility of clinical translation. The abstract highlights the current challenges associated with ex vivo manipulation of autologous Tregs for autoimmune disease treatment, and proposes Cll-RM@aCD4Tn nanoparticles as a more practical alternative. However, the preparation of such nanoparticles at clinically relevant scales may still require large-scale isolation and manipulation of Tregs, potentially undermining the proposed translational advantage. The authors should address this limitation and provide clarification regarding the scalability and feasibility of their approach.

### Reviewer 3

In this interesting manuscript, the authors report the development of DC-CD4 tolerogenic nanoparticle and apply these to varied mouse models of arthritis to demonstrate their their therapeutic potential and draw conclusions about their bio-distribution and mechanism of action. In general the work appears to be technically rigorous and the findings should be of interest to the readership of Nature Communications. However it would be helpful for the authors to consider the following points:
1) In the introduction, the authors mention specific limitations to cell-based therapy approaches but that statement is not referenced. It would be useful to cite at least one definitive review on that topic.
2) The authors tout their tolerogenic DC-CD4 particles as a nano-technology-based strategy that overcomes the limitations of cell-based therapy. However, as outlined in Figure 1, their method still relies on the extraction, manipulation, and re-infusion of cells. Importantly, use of extracellular vesicles in place was less effective. The authors should fully elaborate why their workflow generates a tolerogenic product with fewer limitations than competing methods (both cell based and completely synthetic nanoparticles, as described by Steve Miller and others). Moving beyond inbred mice, DC-CD4 particles could perhaps be manufactured in an autologous or non-autologous manner. Which approach would be the most promising to pursue?
3) A clearer schematic explaining the sequential steps for making the nanoparticles is needed.
4) The rationale for comparing Tn vs Te is not clear. Was this an original hope to develop a cell free therapy that did not come to fruition?
5) It is not obvious why Tn mediated antigen delivery increases surface display of the CII peptide so dramatically. The authors should discuss the mechanism for that increase.
6) Figure 2n showns mRNA levels of TNFa and TGFb. In the conclusion of this section, it is stated that secretion of anti-inflammatory cytokines is enhanced. Can TNFa and TGFb protein be measured in addition to mRNA levels?
7) The meaning of the sentence in lines 202-203 is unclear. This should be revised.
8) The data presented in Figure 3 E and F appears to lack a statistical analysis.
9) In section 4 of the results, localization of NPs is followed for 7 days. Is localization in the lymph nodes still observed beyond 7 days? Knowing this may be important to discern whether the NPs could function as a one time treatment, or if recurrent treatment would be required.
10) In section 5, it is unclear why key experiments were performed using Ova 323-339 rather than the CII peptide. Could similar results be obtained with the autoantigenic peptide?
11) The KEGG pathway data discussed in section 6 does not seem that informative. Are there other published transcript signatures that might be better suited to this analysis?
12) The fluorescence image in figure 6 A is difficult to read.
13) in section 7, mice are sacrificed 14 days post treatment. If mice are kept for longer; does the disease come back?
14) The promising results from different versions of the arthritis model are impressive. However, it must be mentioned that pre-conditioning and prevention settings are easier to mitigate than established disease.
15) The adoptive transfer experiments are very good work and conclude the result section nicely.
16) The paper would benefit from having a discussion section, where the discussion points requested above could be included, along with brief comments about further testing and potential translation of this technology.
